Conquistador—Spanish for conqueror—refers to the Spanish military adventurers and soldiers who conquered vast territories in the Americas in the sixteenth century. They toppled the Aztec and Inca empires and established Spanish colonial rule across Mesoamerica and South America. Armed with steel weapons, horses, and a willingness to commit atrocities, conquistadores like Hernan Cortes and Francisco Pizarro transformed the geopolitical map, enslaved millions of indigenous peoples, and initiated the demographic catastrophe of disease and colonization that reshaped the Americas forever. Conquistadores were typically Spanish soldiers of fortune, religious zealots, and ambitious adventurers seeking wealth, land, and honor. Spain officially sanctioned conquests through encomienda grants—permits to conquer territory and extract indigenous labor. Hernan Cortes conquered the Aztec Empire from 1519 to 1521 with fewer than six hundred men by exploiting indigenous political divisions, indigenous fears of European technology, and relentless violence. The conquest triggered epidemics that killed far more than Spanish swords. Francisco Pizarro conquered the Inca Empire from 1532 to 1572 with similar tactics. Small Spanish forces leveraged internal Incan conflicts, captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa, and dominated through superior military technology and indigenous allies seeking to overthrow Incan rule. Conquistadores established encomienda—a labor system that enslaved indigenous peoples under the pretense of Christian conversion. It was slavery in all but name, with workers laboring to death in mines extracting silver for Spanish wealth. The conquistador era depended on indigenous labor and knowledge. Spanish forces relied on indigenous guides, porters, and warriors who outnumbered Spaniards by orders of magnitude. Indigenous intermediaries translated and negotiated. Without them, conquests would have been impossible. The demographic consequence was catastrophic. Disease introduced by Europeans—smallpox and measles—killed an estimated ninety percent of the indigenous population within a century. This plague preceded Spanish conquest in many regions, weakening indigenous resistance and enabling Spanish dominance.
